title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 9
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Gravitational Waves and Modern Astronomy
passages.text:
Gravitational waves represent one of the most remarkable discoveries in modern physics. First predicted by Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity in 1916 as a consequence of his equations describing spacetime and gravity, gravitational waves remained purely theoretical for nearly a century. Only in 2015, with the direct detection of gravitational waves from the merger of two black holes, did scientists confirm their existence experimentally. This confirmation culminated a decades-long international effort and opened an entirely new window onto the universe.

Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of spacetime itself, emanating from accelerating massive objects. When massive bodies such as neutron stars or black holes orbit each other, they continuously emit gravitational waves that carry energy away from the system. This energy loss causes the objects to gradually spiral inward until they finally collide and merge, releasing a final enormous burst of gravitational radiation. The collision itself generates gravitational waves of tremendous amplitude — spacetime itself oscillates as these waves propagate outward at the speed of light. Despite their enormous power, gravitational waves from distant sources are extraordinarily weak by the time they reach Earth, requiring extraordinarily sensitive instruments to detect.

The detection of gravitational waves required technological breakthroughs. The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, consists of two facilities in the United States with laser interferometers spanning four kilometres in length. These instruments work by splitting a laser beam into two perpendicular arms and recombining the beams after they reflect from mirrors at the end of each arm. When gravitational waves pass through, they alter the lengths of these arms by an infinitesimal amount — a change of merely one ten-thousandth the diameter of a proton. The interferometer detects this minute change in the interference pattern of the recombined beams, allowing scientists to infer the passage of gravitational waves.

Since the first confirmed detection in 2015, LIGO and the European Virgo detector have recorded dozens of gravitational wave events, mostly from black hole mergers but also from collisions of neutron stars. The 2017 detection of gravitational waves from merging neutron stars was particularly significant because it allowed astronomers to detect electromagnetic radiation — light of all wavelengths — from the same event, creating the first multi-messenger astronomical observation. This simultaneous detection of gravitational waves and light provided unprecedented information about the physics of neutron star collisions and confirmed predictions that such collisions produce heavy elements like gold and platinum through nuclear fusion.

Gravitational wave astronomy promises to revolutionise astrophysics. Because gravitational waves travel unobstructed through dust and gas that obscure ordinary light, they allow scientists to observe events and objects previously invisible to traditional telescopes. Observations of gravitational waves from primordial black holes could illuminate the nature of dark matter, one of the universe's greatest mysteries. Future gravitational wave observatories, including the proposed Einstein Telescope and the space-based LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna), will possess unprecedented sensitivity and could detect gravitational waves from the very earliest moments of the universe, potentially providing insights into the Big Bang itself.

passages.title: The History of Vaccination
passages.text:
Vaccination, the practice of deliberately introducing a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen into the body to stimulate immune system response and provide protection against disease, represents one of humanity's greatest public health achievements. While the principle of exposure to mild disease to build immunity dates back to ancient times, the scientific foundation of vaccination was established only in the late eighteenth century through the pioneering work of Edward Jenner, an English physician.

Jenner's innovation was deceptively simple yet revolutionary. He noticed that milkmaids exposed to cowpox, a mild disease similar to smallpox, appeared immune to smallpox itself. In 1796, Jenner tested this observation by deliberately infecting a young boy, James Phipps, with cowpox material through a cut in his skin. After the boy recovered, Jenner inoculated him with material from a smallpox lesion — a procedure that would normally cause severe disease or death. Phipps remained healthy, confirming that cowpox exposure provided protection against smallpox. Jenner called this process 'vaccination,' derived from 'vacca,' the Latin word for cow. His success sparked a revolution in medical practice that spread rapidly across Europe and beyond.

The immunological principle underlying vaccination is the adaptive immune system's ability to remember pathogens. When the body encounters a weakened or inactive pathogen, the adaptive immune system produces antibodies and activates specialised immune cells known as memory cells. These memory cells persist for years or decades, sometimes for life, remaining primed to respond rapidly and effectively when the same pathogen is encountered again in its virulent form. This mechanism explains why individuals typically need only one or a few vaccinations to develop long-term immunity. Some vaccines provide lifelong protection, while others require periodic booster doses to maintain adequate immunity levels.

The nineteenth and twentieth centuries witnessed dramatic improvements in vaccine development. Live attenuated vaccines, containing weakened forms of pathogens, proved effective against diseases like measles and polio. Inactivated vaccines, made from killed pathogens or their components, offered protection with minimal risk of adverse effects. The development of polio vaccines by Jonas Salk and Albert Sabin in the 1950s, followed by vaccines for rubella, mumps, and hepatitis, transformed childhood mortality rates globally. The eradication of smallpox in 1980, achieved through a coordinated international vaccination campaign, remains humanity's greatest victory against infectious disease and demonstrates vaccination's potential to eliminate diseases permanently from human populations.

Modern vaccine development employs sophisticated technologies including recombinant DNA techniques and mRNA technology. The mRNA vaccines developed against COVID-19 represent a breakthrough in vaccine design, using messenger RNA to instruct cells to produce viral proteins that trigger immune response without introducing any virus into the body. These vaccines were developed and tested with unprecedented speed, validated through rigorous clinical trials, and have prevented millions of deaths from COVID-19. Ongoing research continues to expand the applications of vaccination, including development of vaccines against cancers caused by viral pathogens and therapeutic vaccines designed to treat existing infections rather than prevent them.

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasises Einstein's prediction (A), the technological breakthrough of detection (C), and future astronomical applications (E).
options: A. Gravitational waves were predicted by Einstein but not directly detected until 2015.
B. Gravitational waves can only be detected from black hole mergers.
C. LIGO's laser interferometer technology enabled detection of minute spacetime distortions.
D. Gravitational waves travel faster than the speed of light.
E. Gravitational wave astronomy will enable observation of previously hidden cosmic objects and phenomena.
F. All gravitational waves detected thus far have come from events within our solar system.
